Eli5, when I write a file to my hard drive, what is actually happening? (Assuming hdd not ssd).

Basically theres a little magnetic disc in the hard drive, and it's spinning. When you write a file, there's a little read/write magnetic head that reads the magnetic coding of the disc. The head then proceeds to flip a bunch of bits on the disc and boom.

It's probably way more complicated, but this is all I've got.

There is a file system, where files are organized in blocks. Sort of a notebook with pages. At the beginning it will write an entry for that file pointing to the first block(s) of that file.

The blocks are mapped to the HDD. So when you want to write that file, the HDD head will go on a certain track (head movement is extremely fast and precise) and write at a certain section.

The HDD head writes data using current that generates a magnetic field. The magnetic field is stored in the material covering the disk platters.

To read back a file, you place the head over the same track, and measure a very small current change has you pass over changing magnetic field. The magnetic field is changing because the disk is spinning under the head. You the get a signal and time/location. From this you do signal processing to best guess what was written there. (Some signal processing was also done during writting so that it would be easier to retrieve).

My take on it is that as the magnetizable disk spins under the read/write head, bits get magnetized to negative and positive (magnetic poles). There are extra bits written for redundancy to detect and correct for errors. As far as the operating system goes, it probably just keeps the file in memory for awhile if the hard disk is busy, else it looks in the file directory blocks (think of a table of contents for a book) and finds some unused space to write the bits into.
